q: Coonawarra lies some eighty kilometres from the Southern Ocean and among the more southerly of mainland Australia's vineyard regions, so the season is long and the picking late. What does that slowness give the fruit?
opts: Reliable botrytis in the majority of vintages
Skins thin enough to remove any need for maceration
A higher sugar level than any warmer region can reach
Time for tannin and flavour to ripen while the acidity is still intact
exp: Sugar and flavour ripen at different rates, and a long cool season lets the second catch up with the first. Fast-ripened fruit in a hot region gives alcohol before the tannin has softened, and escaping that trade is the whole point of a cool Cabernet site.

q: Coonawarra, Padthaway and Wrattonbully all sit inside one South Australian zone, named for the rock they have in common. Which zone?
exp: The Limestone Coast also takes in Mount Benson, Robe and Mount Gambier, all standing on the same ancient seabed. Fleurieu covers McLaren Vale and Langhorne Creek, and Mount Lofty Ranges covers the Adelaide Hills and Clare.

q: Some seventy kilometres north of Coonawarra, on the same limestone, a flatter region was opened up by large companies in the 1960s and became a major source of Chardonnay for national brands. Which region?
exp: Padthaway was developed as a fruit source rather than as a cellar-door destination, and much of its crop has always left the region in a tanker. Wrattonbully, lying between it and Coonawarra, came later and leans red.

q: An hour's drive east of Melbourne, on hillsides first planted in 1838, growers make Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and traditional-method sparkling. Which region?
exp: The Yarra Valley is Victoria's oldest region and among its coolest, and it spreads across enough altitude and aspect to give quite different wines within one name. Cool-climate Shiraz and Cabernet are made there too, but the Burgundian pair define it.

q: A strip of land jutting south from Melbourne has water on three sides, so no vineyard on it stands far from the sea. Which region?
exp: Port Phillip Bay, Western Port and Bass Strait surround the Mornington Peninsula and hold its temperature inside a narrow band. Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris account for most of what is planted, in small holdings farmed intensively.

q: Central Victorian vineyards sit on a narrow ridge of deep red soil weathered from Cambrian greenstone half a billion years old, and the ridge has become a byword for powerful dark Shiraz. Which region?
exp: The Cambrian ridge runs north to south for some fifty kilometres and its soil holds water well, so the vines ripen steadily rather than under stress. Heathcote Shiraz is dense and dark but keeps a cooler, bluer-fruited edge than a Barossa version.

q: A tiny glass arrives at the end of dinner almost black and syrupy, smelling of raisins, rose and orange marmalade, fortified and matured for decades in old wood in hot north-east Victoria. What is it?
exp: Rutherglen Muscat comes from Muscat a Petits Grains Rouges left on the vine until it raisins, then fortified and aged through fierce inland summers. Heat and slow evaporation concentrate it further, and the oldest material is blended back into younger wine in a solera-like fashion.

q: Rutherglen grades its fortified Muscat on a four-step ladder of rising age and concentration. Which step sits at the top?
exp: The ladder runs Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare, each demanding a greater average age and a higher concentration than the rung below. It is a scheme run by the producers themselves rather than a legal category, and it is one of the very few age classifications in Australian wine.

q: A district in western Victoria built its name on peppery Shiraz and on a sparkling red made from the same grape, and its cellars were tunnelled out of the rock by out-of-work gold miners in the 1860s. Which region?
exp: The Grampians, long known as Great Western, sits high enough for a genuinely cool season, so its Shiraz is medium-bodied and spicy rather than broad and sweet. The drives cut into the rock still hold bottles for the region's sparkling reds.

q: One white Rhone variety found an unlikely stronghold in central Victoria, where some of the oldest surviving plantings anywhere are still worked. Which variety?
exp: Marsanne reached the Goulburn Valley in the nineteenth century and stayed, and vines put in during the 1920s are still cropping at Nagambie Lakes. Young it is quiet and lemony; after a decade in bottle it turns to honeysuckle and toast, which is why the good examples repay cellaring.

q: A ten-year-old white shows toast, honey and lanolin, has never been near oak, and left the winery at barely eleven percent alcohol. Which region and grape produced it?
exp: Hunter Semillon is picked early at low sugar and high acid, fermented cool in tank and bottled young, when it tastes of very little. The toast develops entirely in bottle with no oak involved at any stage, and no other region makes anything closely comparable.

q: Rain at harvest, high humidity and cloud through the ripening season would be a catastrophe across most of Australia, and are simply normal in one of its oldest fine wine regions. Which?
exp: The Hunter lies at a subtropical latitude with summer-dominant rainfall arriving off the Pacific, and picking often begins in January. The cloud that comes with the humidity is also a mercy, since it moderates a sun that would otherwise scorch the fruit.

q: Medium-bodied, earthy and leathery rather than dense and sweet, the classic red of the Hunter is made from the same variety as the Barossa's blockbusters. Which variety?
exp: Cloud, humidity and an early harvest leave the Hunter with lower sugar and softer extract than the Barossa draws from the same grape. It was sold through most of the twentieth century as Hunter River Burgundy, which says a good deal about how differently it drinks.

q: One New South Wales region writes a minimum height above sea level into its Geographical Indication, so land below that line may not use the name. Which region?
exp: Only vineyards at or above six hundred metres may be labelled Orange, and the highest sit well beyond nine hundred on the slopes of an extinct volcano. It is an unusual clause in a system that normally draws a boundary on a map and says nothing about the land inside it.

q: A hot, flat, irrigated district in inland New South Wales is famous for one wine that has nothing to do with volume: a sweet golden botrytis-affected Semillon. Which district?
exp: Fog rising off the irrigation channels around Griffith brings botrytis to fruit that would stay clean in so dry a climate, and the sweet wines that result are among Australia's finest. The same district supplies vast quantities of everyday wine, which is why its reputation lags its best bottles.

q: A promontory at the far south-western corner of the continent has ocean on three sides and built its reputation on Cabernet Sauvignon grown in gravelly soil. Which region?
exp: Margaret River runs between Cape Naturaliste and Cape Leeuwin, with the Indian Ocean to the west and the Southern Ocean to the south. Its Cabernet is structured and cassis-scented, and it is the wine by which the region is measured.
